From the experimental testing data, the initial temperature, inlet HTF temperature and inlet HTF mass flow rate was provided as inputs to the model. Figure 50 overlays the transient results predicted by the numerical model with experimental data for (a) HTF temperature at the sulfur TES outlet, (b) bulk sulfur temperature, and (c) heat rate over three charge-discharge cycles. Two instruments were used together to measure and record the temperature: a K-type thermocouple and a data acquisition (DAQ) module. Each instrument introduces an error in the temperature measurements, which are systematic errors. Therefore, the total uncertainty in the temperature measurement was calculated by summing the individual uncertainties of these instruments. For the temperature range of 200–310 °C, the total uncertainty in the temperature measurements is ±3.2 °C. From Figure 50, it is observed that the model prediction is in good agreement with experimental results with mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) below 1 percent for both HTF exit temperature and sulfur bulk temperature, and 9.6 percent for heat rate. The corresponding root-mean squared error (RMSE) values are 1.3 oC, 2.5 oC and 5.5 kW, respectively. Page 73 of 87 DE-EE0009329 Element 16 Technologies, Inc. SVM uses 150,000 lb/h, 200 psig (200 oC) steam for their continuous process heat requirement that equates to a constant heat demand rate of 150 MMBTU/h (𝑄̇ = 45 MWt). 𝐼𝑃𝐻 Figure 2 shows the system configuration considered for the analysis. The solar field array uses commercially proven parabolic trough technology that concentrates sunlight to heat thermal oil heat transfer fluid (HTF) flowing through the receiver tubes. Excess heat during peak solar period is stored in the sulfur TES and dispatched as needed to meet the constant process heat requirement. Due to the variable nature of solar insolation and the dynamic behavior of solar thermal system, the existing natural gas (NG) boiler would be used as a back-up system to ensure the thermal load is always met. Hourly simulation for a year was carried out to evaluate the annual performance of the hybrid solar-TES-boiler system illustrated in Figure 2. The solar field performance model used in this simulation was developed and validated against results from NREL’s system advisor model (SAM) [41] in Task 2. The sulfur TES performance model and its validation against experimental results from pilot prototype testing were presented in the previous section.
